author: Claude (EFL materials writer role)
basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.

slides.1: Good morning. Does every student in Taiwan get the same computers and internet? Today we study SDG 4 on the screen. Our online classrooms look modern, but are they fair?
slides.2: So what does SDG 4 mean online? Every child should reach the same lessons, wherever they live. But do our schools teach us to stay safe on the internet?
slides.3: Taiwan is famous for its computer chips, so schools fill their classrooms with tablets and apps. But the birth rate keeps falling. Do these tools really help every child learn?
slides.4: Here is the first problem. City students have fast internet at home. In some country schools the line is slow, so online lessons are difficult. Is that fair to them?
slides.5: Next, think about fake news. Many of us live on social media, and false stories fly past all day. Few students stop to check them, so our thinking gets lazy.
slides.6: Safety is the next worry. Online bullying is growing, and it follows children home at night. Their mind pays the price. Is our school system doing enough to protect them?
slides.7: Now the good news. The government started a plan called "tablets for every student". Thousands of country children now hold their own device, so a lesson can reach them at home.
slides.8: The government also pays for free study websites. A family with little money can still get good lessons at home. That makes the game fairer for us all.
slides.9: Our teachers also learn new digital skills. But when a class stares at screens every day, does the learning get better? Or do they just get tired?
slides.10: So what is the answer? Schools now teach media literacy. Children learn to spot a fake story and to check where a fact came from, before they share it.
slides.11: Some schools now use AI helpers too. The program watches how you work and then sets homework that fits you. Your lesson finally feels like your own.
slides.12: In the mountains, a van brings the lab to the village. It carries laptops, robots and coding games. Children who live far away still get to build something.
slides.13: Why does this matter? Taiwan sells about 500 billion dollars of goods a year, and most of it is technology. Safe and skilled internet users can also help fix world problems.
slides.14: But there is a cost. Internet addiction is rising fast, and many students stay online all night. Their body and their mood suffer. We have to change that habit.
slides.15: If we ignore this gap, talent will simply drain away. As college students, we should ask one hard question. Are our schools ready for work that AI keeps changing?
slides.16: Good digital lessons make a country strong. If we do not change, Taiwan will fall behind. Media literacy must grow, because the internet will never get simpler.
slides.17: So where are we now? Taiwan has put a screen in almost every classroom, and that is real progress. But fair use of it is still missing.
slides.18: Look a little deeper. Many devices are good, but clear thinking is better. We need students who make things on a screen, not students who only watch it.
slides.19: In the future, digital rights must cover everyone. That includes the groups we usually forget. Ask for lessons that show us how the internet really works in real life.
slides.20: Teach an older neighbor to use a phone, or help a younger student online. Together, we can build a digital future that leaves nobody out. Let's start today.
